nameStory: Chestnut blight gets its name from the devastating disease it causes in American chestnut trees. The word 'blight' comes from an old English term meaning 'to wither' or 'to damage,' perfectly describing how this fungus kills the bark and eventually the entire tree. This tiny fungus earned its ominous name by wiping out billions of majestic chestnuts across eastern North America in just a few decades.
description: Chestnut blight is a microscopic fungus that causes one of the most devastating tree diseases in North American history. You won't see the fungus itself without a microscope, but you'll definitely notice what it does to chestnut trees. It creates sunken, cracked areas of dead bark called cankers that girdle and kill branches or entire trunks. The fungus produces tiny, orange to reddish-brown fruiting bodies that look like little bumps pushing through the dead bark.

idTips.label: Sunken cankers
idTips.description: Look for depressed, cracked areas of bark that feel rough and brittle to the touch, often with a distinct border between healthy and diseased tissue

idTips.label: Orange fruiting bodies
idTips.description: Tiny orange to reddish-brown bumps, smaller than a pinhead, scattered across the dead bark surface - they feel slightly raised and gritty

idTips.label: Bark texture
idTips.description: Infected bark becomes dry and crumbly, peeling away in strips that sound papery when touched, unlike healthy bark which stays firmly attached

idTips.label: Wilting foliage
idTips.description: Leaves above infected areas turn yellow then brown but often remain attached through winter, creating a flag-like appearance

idTips.label: Girdling pattern
idTips.description: Cankers wrap around branches or trunks, creating a distinct line where everything above dies while below remains healthy

habitat: Found wherever American chestnut trees grow in New England's forests, from sea level to mountain slopes up to 3,000 feet. Most commonly seen in mixed hardwood forests, old pastures with remnant chestnuts, and areas where chestnut root systems send up new sprouts. The fungus thrives in the warm, humid conditions of New England summers.

seasonality.spring: New infections often begin as small, discolored patches on bark as temperatures warm and humidity increases.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when orange fruiting bodies are most visible and cankers expand rapidly in the heat and moisture.
seasonality.fall: Cankers become more obvious as infected branches fail to drop their leaves normally, creating telltale brown flags against the autumn landscape.
seasonality.winter: Dead, flagged leaves remain attached to infected branches, making diseased trees easy to spot against bare forest backgrounds.

funFact: This fungus accidentally eliminated what was once every fourth tree in eastern American forests - American chestnuts that could live 500+ years and grow wider than cars - yet the trees refuse to give up, continuously sending up new shoots from still-living root systems a century after the original giants died.
confusionNotes: Other tree diseases can cause similar-looking cankers, but chestnut blight specifically targets chestnuts and produces distinctive tiny orange fruiting bodies. Remember: if it's killing a chestnut and has orange bumps, it's probably the blight that changed American forests forever.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this with horse chestnuts (buckeyes) or water chestnuts - American chestnuts are in an entirely different plant family. The devastating chestnut blight fungus was accidentally introduced from Asia around 1904 and represents one of ecology's most dramatic examples of how non-native species can reshape entire ecosystems.
compareHints: Since chestnut blight is the only Cryphonectria species commonly found in New England, compare it with other canker-causing fungi like Nectria species. Unlike Nectria's bright red or pink fruiting bodies, chestnut blight produces orange to reddish-brown bumps. Chestnut blight also specifically targets chestnut trees, while other canker fungi typically affect different tree species.
